title: Detection of Written Content
summary: This detection strategy focuses on written content produced by generative artificial intelligence (AI) for use in deception, such as phishing mail, fake persona profiles, fraudulent invoices, chat messages and documents. It covers technique T1683.001 and matters because text is the cheapest content to generate, so it is the channel where machine scale appears first and in the largest volume. The telemetry that makes it possible is mail body and header metadata, stylometric scoring, text similarity and embedding comparisons across a corpus, document authorship metadata, and outbound requests to public AI writing services from the estate. In practice the strategy fails because generated prose is intended to read naturally, employees use assistants for legitimate work, and text classifiers produce false positives on non native speakers and on heavily templated business writing. The dependable signals are volume, repetition with small variations, and the relationship between sender and recipient.

beginner.definition: Written content means text: email, chat messages, documents and online profiles. This detection looks for text written by artificial intelligence (AI) at machine speed to trick people. It finds campaigns, not one message.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most attacks start with words, such as a message that asks you to sign in somewhere. Writing those messages used to take time and skill. A machine can now produce a huge number of good ones. The volume makes each message harder to check by hand, so you need pattern based detection.
howItWorks: You collect text metadata from mail, chat and document stores. You keep the sender and the timing.
You compare texts with each other to find groups that are almost the same.
You check grammar, tone and length for unusual uniformity across many messages.
You score the text with a language model that estimates machine authorship.
You check the account history. New accounts that send a lot are more interesting.
You alert on the campaign and show several examples side by side.
beginner.example: Think of a market stall selling cakes. One cake that looks perfect means nothing at all. But the seller produces two hundred perfect cakes in five minutes. Every cake is exactly the same size. The single cake was never the clue. The speed and the sameness were.
takeaways: Machine written text is best caught in groups, not one message at a time.
Near duplicates with small changes are a strong sign of automated generation.
Text scoring is only evidence. Account history and volume carry more weight.

objectives: Explain why written text is the most common channel for machine generated deception
Measure near duplication and small variation across a corpus of messages or documents
Apply language model scores to text while stating their accuracy limits clearly
Correlate text similarity findings with newly created accounts and first contact recipients
Read document authorship and revision metadata to look for signs of automated production
Produce a campaign level alert that presents representative samples rather than every match
dataSources: Mail gateway records containing message body text hash, body length, language, subject and send timestamp
Collaboration and chat platform audit records with message bodies or body hashes, sender account and channel membership
Document management or file share metadata recording author, revision count and creation to modification interval
Language model authorship or perplexity scores stored as enrichment against each message or document identifier
Outbound web proxy logs showing POST requests to public generative artificial intelligence writing service endpoints
logic: The pattern is a group of texts that share structure and phrasing while differing in the details that a human writer would naturally vary. You correlate body hashes, similarity scores and authorship scores across messages, and join them to sender account age, sending volume for the same window, and whether the recipient has prior contact with the sender. The malicious case is dozens or hundreds of messages produced in a short interval, each nearly identical apart from names, amounts or links, from accounts created within days of the campaign, targeting recipients outside the sender's normal contact graph. The benign case is business correspondence built from a shared template by an established sender with an existing relationship. Similarity plus account age plus missing relationship history is the combination that holds up.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Near Duplicate Written Content From Accounts Outside Normal Contact Graph
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: email
# detection:
#   selection:
#     body_similarity: > 0.9
#     message_count_1h: > 20
#     sender_reputation: 'new'
#   filter_known:
#     sender_domain|endswith:
#       - '.example.com'
#       - '.trusted-partner.example'
#   condition: selection and not filter_known
# level: medium
falsePositives: Recruitment agencies sending individually addressed but structurally identical candidate submissions
Accounts payable teams circulating the same reminder text to many suppliers about outstanding invoices
Student or trainee exercises that produce many similar documents from one shared prompt or template
Internal communications teams distributing a newsletter with only the recipient name changed
Employees using an approved writing assistant to rewrite routine replies, which increases phrase similarity
tuningNotes: Build the comparison corpus from your own mail and document stores for at least thirty days, then set the similarity threshold just above the level your normal templates reach. Filter bodies that come from known bulk senders, and group by campaign identifier so the queue shows one item per burst. Scope the first version to external inbound mail and to file shares that hold customer facing documents, then extend to chat once the noise level is understood. Filtering on high similarity alone will miss a single well crafted message, so keep user reporting and link reputation detections running alongside this rule.
